    Getting Started

    Last updated on 2026-11-06 | Edit this page

    This page walks you through everything you need to do before Session 1. Please finish it at least a day ahead. The downloads are large, and we will not have time to troubleshoot installations during the workshop.

    It takes about 30 to 45 minutes, most of it waiting for downloads. Use a reliable internet connection (not a conference hotspot), and plug in your laptop.

    Checklist

    What you need

    • A laptop running Windows, macOS, or Linux that you are allowed to install software on. If it is managed by your institution, see the troubleshooting notes at the bottom of this page.
    • About 5 GB of free disk space and, we recommend, 8 GB of memory (RAM). The notebook loads a full deployment of instrument data.
    • Three tools, which this page helps you install:
      1. git, for version control
      2. uv, which installs Python and manages your packages
      3. A free GitHub account
    • The workshop starter files (a notebook and two data files, about 1 GB in total).

    You do not need to install Python, Jupyter, Anaconda, or conda separately. uv takes care of Python and every package we use.

    Step 0: Open a terminal

    Most of the commands on this page are typed into a terminal, a window where you type commands instead of clicking. Copy each command exactly, press Enter, and wait for it to finish before typing the next one.

    • Windows: use Git Bash, a terminal that is installed together with git in Step 1. Open the Start menu, type Git Bash, and open it. Use Git Bash for every command in this workshop (not PowerShell or Command Prompt), so that the commands are the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Because Git Bash comes with git, Windows users should do Step 1 first.
    • macOS: press Cmd + Space, type Terminal, and press Enter.
    • Linux: press Ctrl + Alt + T, or search your applications for “Terminal”.

    Step 1: Install git

    Download and run the installer from git-scm.com/download/win, accepting the default options. This installs both git and Git Bash. (If you use WinGet, running winget install --id Git.Git -e in PowerShell does the same thing.)

    When it finishes, open Git Bash from the Start menu. Type all the commands on this page there. You can also right-click inside any folder in File Explorer and choose Open Git Bash here (on Windows 11 it may be under Show more options), which opens Git Bash already in that folder.

    Git is often already installed. Type git --version in Terminal. If git is missing, macOS offers to install the “command line developer tools”; accept the offer and wait for it to finish.

    Install git with your package manager, for example sudo apt install git (Debian, Ubuntu) or sudo dnf install git (Fedora).

    On macOS and Linux, close your terminal and open a new one. On Windows, you are already in Git Bash. Check that it worked:

    BASH 

    git --version

    OUTPUT 

    git version 2.47.0

    Your version number will differ. Any recent version is fine.

    Next, tell git who you are. Git stamps this on every commit you make, and it will refuse to commit in Session 2 without it. Use your own name and email:

    BASH 

    git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"

    Step 2: Create a GitHub account

    If you do not already have one, create a free account at github.com/signup. Session 2 is about building a repository you can share, and GitHub is where most people host one.

    Step 3: Install uv

    uv is the one tool we use for Python itself, for environments, and for packages.

    In Git Bash, run:

    BASH 

    powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

    This uses Windows’ built-in PowerShell only to run uv’s installer; you keep typing in Git Bash. Or, if you use WinGet, run winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e in Git Bash instead.

    In Terminal, run:

    BASH 

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

    Or, if you use Homebrew: brew install uv.

    In a terminal, run:

    BASH 

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

    Close your terminal (on Windows, every Git Bash window) and open a new one. This step is easy to skip and the most common reason for a “command not found” error right after installing. Then check that uv works:

    BASH 

    uv --version

    OUTPUT 

    uv 0.11.32

    Your version number will differ. Any recent version is fine.

    Step 4: Download the starter files

    Download starter-files.zip from the lesson’s Releases page and unzip it to a folder you will be able to find again, for example a new folder called workshop in your Documents folder.

    Caution

    Use the zip file from the Releases page. Do not use GitHub’s green “Code → Download ZIP” button for this: it does not include the large data files.

    After unzipping you should have:

    starter-files/
├── README.md
├── first_analysis.ipynb
└── data/
    ├── gi01sumo_nsif_ctd.nc
    └── gi01sumo_nsif_dosta.nc

    The two .nc files are real OOI data, so they are large: roughly 120 MB for the CTD file and 800 MB for the DOSTA file. If either file is only a few hundred bytes, you have a text placeholder and not the data. Download the zip again.

    Step 5: Run the dress rehearsal

    This step downloads every package we use, so that the workshop itself does not have to. It also proves that your setup works end to end.

    1. In your terminal, move into the starter-files folder. Replace the path below with wherever you unzipped it:

    BASH 

    cd ~/Documents/workshop/starter-files

    On Windows, Git Bash understands ~ as your user folder (C:\Users\yourname) and uses forward slashes. If your Documents folder is synced by OneDrive, the path is probably ~/OneDrive/Documents/workshop/starter-files. A drive letter is written like /c/, for example /c/Users/yourname/Documents. The easiest route is to open the starter-files folder in File Explorer and choose Open Git Bash here.

    2. Start JupyterLab with all the packages the workshop uses:

    BASH 

    uv run --no-project --with jupyterlab --with xarray --with netCDF4 --with pandas --with numpy --with matplotlib jupyter lab

    The first time, this prints many “Downloading…” lines and can take several minutes. That is normal. When it finishes, JupyterLab opens in your web browser. If no browser window appears, look in the terminal for a line starting with http://localhost:8888/lab?token= and copy that whole address into your browser.

    3. In JupyterLab, open first_analysis.ipynb from the file list on the left. Click the first cell and press Shift + Enter to run it, then do the same for the second cell. Neither should print an error.

    4. Click an empty cell at the bottom, type the following, and press Shift + Enter:

    PYTHON 

    print(ctd.sizes)
print(dosta.sizes)

    You should see two lines, each reporting a number of points along time, something like Frozen({'time': 1234567}). The numbers will differ from this example; what matters is that both lines print and neither is an error.

    5. To shut JupyterLab down, go back to the terminal and press Ctrl + C. If it asks whether to shut down, type y and press Enter.

    6. Run the command from step 2 again. This time JupyterLab should start within a few seconds, because uv reuses what it already downloaded.

    Discussion

    What do --no-project and --with mean?

    --with jupyterlab (and the others) asks uv to build a temporary environment that contains those packages and run the command inside it. --no-project tells uv not to look for a pyproject.toml in the current folder, because you have not made a project yet. In Session 2 you will create one, and it will record these packages for you.

    Step 6 (optional): Pick an editor

    You can do the whole workshop in JupyterLab. If you already prefer another editor, such as VS Code or PyCharm, that is fine too. VS Code with its Python and Jupyter extensions works well for editing the .py modules you will write next to your notebook.

    You are ready when…

    Checklist
    • git --version prints a version number
    • git config --global user.name prints your name
    • uv --version prints a version number
    • You can log in to GitHub
    • You launched JupyterLab from the starter-files folder, ran the first two cells of first_analysis.ipynb, and print(ctd.sizes) worked

    If something on the list does not work and the troubleshooting notes below do not fix it, email the instructors before the workshop. We would much rather sort it out beforehand.

    Troubleshooting

    uv: command not found. Close every terminal window (on Windows, every Git Bash window) and open a new one. The installer changes your search path, and only new terminals see the change.

    The download stalls, fails, or is blocked. Institutional networks and VPNs sometimes block software downloads. Try again off the VPN, or on a different network. If you are on a managed laptop, your IT group may need to allow downloads from astral.sh, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, and github.com. If you cannot install software at all, tell the instructors right away so we can find a workaround.

    Windows: the uv install command says running scripts is disabled. The install command above already bypasses that setting for this one command. If your organization blocks it anyway, use the winget command instead, or ask your IT group.

    JupyterLab does not open in a browser. Copy the http://localhost:8888/... address from the terminal and paste it into your browser. If port 8888 is already in use, JupyterLab picks the next free port and prints that address.

    FileNotFoundError: ... data/gi01sumo_nsif_ctd.nc. JupyterLab was started from the wrong folder. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal, cd into the folder that contains both first_analysis.ipynb and the data folder, and run the launch command again.

    The .nc files are tiny (a few hundred bytes). They are placeholders. See Step 4.

    The kernel died or the computer ran out of memory. Close other programs, especially web browsers with many tabs, and run the cells again. If it keeps happening, tell the instructors which computer and how much memory it has.

    Something else. Copy the full error message from the terminal and send it to the instructors. A screenshot of the whole terminal window is even better.
